extracted.intended_audience: educated readers and literary critics of epic poetry (readers of Milton)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for analysing and appreciating books of an epic poem (here: Milton's Paradise Lost), with recommended categories of attention (description, machinery/speeches, conduct of actors) and principles for diction, characterization, and the use of imagery and devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threefold framework for analysing an epic book
rubrics_metrics.description: We may consider the Beauties of the Fourth Book under three Heads. In the first are those Pictures of Still-Life ... In the next are the Machines, which comprehend the Speeches and Behaviour of the good and bad Angels. In the last is the Conduct of Adam and Eve, who are the Principal Actors in the Poem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When criticising a book of an epic, examine (1) descriptive still-life passages (scenery, objects), (2) the machinery — the speeches and conduct of supernatural or organizing agents, and (3) the moral/dramatic conduct of the principal human actors. The essay treats each head in turn and uses them to account for Milton's successes and faults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply ornamented diction to weak or unactive parts
rubrics_metrics.description: In the Description of Paradise, the Poet has observed Aristotle's Rule of lavishing all the Ornaments of Diction on the weak unactive Parts of the Fable, which are not supported by the Beauty of Sentiments and Characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use more florid, elaborate language where the action is 'weak' or unactive (e.g., landscape/description), reserving restraint where the main sentiments and characters carry the scene. This explains why descriptive passages are often more ornate than action-driven passages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justify length and particularity of description by its dramatic role
rubrics_metrics.description: Tho the Drawings of Gardens, Rivers, Rainbows, and the like dead Pieces of Nature, are justly censured in an Heroic Poem, when they run out into an unnecessary length; the Description of Paradise would have been faulty, had not the Poet been very particular in it, not only as it is the Scene of the Principal Action, but as it is requisite to give us an Idea of that Happiness from which our first Parents fell.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long descriptive passages are permissible only when they serve a necessary dramatic or thematic purpose (e.g., to establish the scene that grounds the principal action). Avoid gratuitous digressions into nature that do not support the poem's central concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make characters' thoughts and speech reflect their setting and station
rubrics_metrics.description: Scarce a Speech of Adam or Eve in the whole Poem, wherein the Sentiments and Allusions are not taken from this their delightful Habitation ... their Thoughts are always Paradisiacal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure characters' diction, imagery, and allusions are consistent with their environment and roles: shepherds' thoughts should be tinctured by woods/fields/rivers; Adam and Eve's speech should continually reflect their paradisal setting. This coherence enhances verisimilitude and thematic unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Raise speeches to reveal internal conflict and moral progression
rubrics_metrics.description: Satan ... is filled with Sentiments different from those which he discovered whilst he was in Hell. The Place inspires him with Thoughts more adapted to it: He reflects ... and breaks forth into a Speech that is softned with several transient Touches of Remorse and Self-accusation: But at length he confirms himself in Impenitence, and in his Design ... This Conflict of Passions is raised with a great deal of Art, as the opening of his Speech to the Sun is very bold and noble.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose important speeches so they show a sequence of inner states (remorse, temptation, reassertion of purpose) rather than flat declarations. A strong opening line can set the tone; the progression should be artfully staged to reveal character and motive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use transformations and surprising circumstances to advance plot and intrigue
rubrics_metrics.description: His bounding over the Walls of Paradise; his sitting in the Shape of a Cormorant upon the Tree of Life ... his alighting among the Herd of Animals ... his transforming himself into different Shapes, in order to hear their Conversation, are Circumstances that give an agreeable Surprize to the Reader, and are devised with great Art, to connect that Series of Adventures in which the Poet has engaged this Artificer of Fraud.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ metamorphosis, disguise, and unexpected situations judiciously to surprise readers and to link episodes into a coherent adventurous sequence. Such devices should be crafted to reveal character (here, Satan as 'Artificer of Fraud') and to propel the narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground extraordinary details in classical/allusive precedent
rubrics_metrics.description: The Thought of Satan's Transformation into a Cormorant, and placing himself on the Tree of Life, seems raised upon that Passage in the Iliad, where two Deities are described, as perching on the Top of an Oak in the shape of Vulturs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allusions to classical models can lend weight and resonance to striking images; use precedent to justify imaginative choices and to situate them within a literary tradition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embed moral meaning beneath literal action
rubrics_metrics.description: His planting himself at the Ear of Eve under the form of a Toad, in order to produce vain Dreams and Imaginations, is a Circumstance of the same Nature; as his starting up in his own Form is wonderfully fine, both in the Literal Description, and in the Moral which is concealed under it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Layer actions so that there is a literal (narrative) level and a concealed moral or symbolic level; effective episodes work on both planes and reward close reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep characters' responses consistent with their established traits
rubrics_metrics.description: His Answer upon his being discovered, and demanded to give an Account of himself, is conformable to the Pride and Intrepidity of his Character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a character is confronted, their replies and conduct should align with the qualities previously ascribed to them (pride, courage, timidity etc.), thereby reinforcing characterization and plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use interactions between characters to reveal moral and aesthetic effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Zephon's Rebuke, with the Influence it had on Satan, is exquisitely Graceful and Moral.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft exchanges (rebukes, remonstrances, replies) so they not only move the plot but also display moral contrasts and aesthetic grace; reactions should have discernible influence and illuminate character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep a punctual journal as a method of self-examination
rubrics_metrics.description: I would, however, recommend to every one of my Readers, the keeping a Journal of their Lives for one Week, and setting down punctually their whole Series of Employments during that Space of Time. This Kind of Self-Examination would give them a true State of themselves, and incline them to consider seriously what they are about.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To discover how one truly spends time and to correct omissions, record daily activities punctually for a week; one day's record will rectify another's omissions and help weigh indifferent actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Private, quiet employments can be more profitable than public action
rubrics_metrics.description: I do not suppose that a Man loses his Time, who is not engaged in publick Affairs, or in an Illustrious Course of Action. On the Contrary, I believe our Hours may very often be more profitably laid out in such Transactions as make no Figure in the World, than in such as are apt to draw upon them the Attention of Mankind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value silent, private pursuits (study, contemplation, habitual small improvements) as legitimate and often superior modes of self-improvement to public, ostentatious activity.
